title: Email & Online Safety Basics in Canada
summary: Spot common scams, choose safer passwords, and know where to report fraud in Canada.
goals: Spot common scams, choose safer passwords, and know where to report fraud in Canada.
introHtml:
Spot common scams, choose safer passwords, and know where to report fraud in Canada.

By the end, learners can: spot common CRA and phishing scams; choose safer password habits; know when not to click; and report fraud to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre (CAFC) and, when needed, the CRA.

lessons.title: What is a scam message?
lessons.html:
A scam message tries to trick you into giving money or private information. It can arrive as a phone call, text, email, or chat. Scammers often pretend to be a bank, a delivery company, or the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA).

Common warning signs:

  • The message says you must act right now or something bad will happen.
  • It asks for gift cards, cryptocurrency, or an Interac e-Transfer to a person you do not know.
  • It asks you to click a link and “sign in” to fix a problem.
  • The spelling or grammar looks odd — but some scams now look very real.

The CRA publishes a clear list of things it will not do. For example, the CRA will not send refunds by e-Transfer or text, will not ask for payment by gift card or cryptocurrency, and will not threaten to arrest or deport you in an aggressive call. If a “CRA” caller does these things, hang up. Look up a real CRA phone number yourself later, or sign in only through official pages that start with canada.ca.

Remember: Feeling scared or rushed is a tool scammers use. Slow down. Ask a trusted person or your adult learning centre before you send money or personal details.

lessons.title: CRA phone and text scams
lessons.html:
Scammers love to pretend they are the CRA because many people worry about taxes and benefits.

Phone scams: Someone may call and say you owe money, or that you will be arrested. They may even make the caller ID look like a real number (“spoofing”). The CRA may contact people for real reasons, but it will not use the extreme threats and payment methods listed on its scam pages. If you did not expect the call, hang up. Later, find the CRA contact page on canada.ca and call that number yourself — or sign in to your CRA account through canada.ca.

Text and chat scams: The CRA says it does not start tax conversations by text or by apps like WhatsApp. Texts for multi-factor sign-in are different and only happen if you set that up. A text that offers a refund, asks you to reply “YES,” or sends a “deposit” link is a red flag.

What the CRA emails look like (high level): If you signed up for email notifications, the CRA may email to say you have mail inside your CRA account. Those emails should not ask you to reply with passwords or to enter banking details in the email itself. When in doubt, type canada.ca in your browser and sign in from there. Do not click the link in a surprise message.

If you already shared information or see strange changes on your tax account, report it using the CRA’s scam/identity theft reporting page and also tell the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

lessons.title: Phishing emails and fake websites
lessons.html:
Phishing means a fake message that tries to get your passwords, SIN, banking details, or to make you install harmful software. The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre (CAFC) warns that phishing can look like a bank, a store, or a government agency.

Typical tricks:

  • “Your package could not be delivered — click here.”
  • “Your account will close today — update now.”
  • “You have a tax refund waiting — sign in.”
  • A QR code in a surprise email or poster that leads to a fake sign-in page.

Fake websites often use look-alike addresses: extra words, odd endings (.info, .su), or small spelling changes. CRA guidance: official pages start with canada.ca or end with cra-arc.gc.ca. When unsure, do not click. Type the address yourself.

Quick habits:

  1. Do not click links or open attachments in surprise messages.
  2. Do not “confirm” passwords by email or text.
  3. Hover or long-press a link on your phone to preview the address (still be careful).
  4. If you clicked by mistake, change your password on the real site, turn on stronger sign-in if available, and watch your accounts. Report the attempt.

Reporting helps others. CAFC wants reports even if you did not lose money.

lessons.title: Strong passwords and passphrases
lessons.html:
Your password is a key to email, banking, and government accounts. Get Cyber Safe (Government of Canada) recommends unique passwords or passphrases for each important account.

Passphrase tip: Use four or more random words and at least about 15 characters when you can (for example, a made-up phrase you can picture). Random words are stronger than a pet’s name or your birthday.

If you must use a shorter password style, aim for length, a mix of character types, and something that is not a common word.

Do:

  • Use a different password for email and banking.
  • Consider a password manager if you and your tutor are comfortable with one.
  • Turn on multi-factor authentication (a second step, like a code) when the site offers it.

Do not:

  • Share passwords.
  • Send a password by email or text because someone asked.
  • Reuse the same password everywhere — one breach can open many doors.

If a site is breached, change that password and any other site where you reused it. Practise creating a passphrase on paper first (keep the paper private), then type it into a real account only when you are ready.

If one account is stolen, others are harder to open

lessons.title: How to report fraud in Canada
lessons.html:
If you spot a scam — or you already shared information — reporting helps you and your community.

1. Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre (CAFC)
Report online or call toll-free 1-888-495-8501. Report even if you did not lose money. Keep notes: date, phone numbers, emails, screenshots, and what they asked for.

2. Canada Revenue Agency (CRA)
If the scam involved your tax or benefits account, or you see unauthorized changes, use the CRA’s report-a-scam / identity theft options (online form or phone). They can help place protections on your account.

3. Local police
Especially important if you lost money. Ask for a file number and keep it.

4. Your bank or credit union
Call them quickly if you sent money or shared banking passwords. Ask about next steps and monitoring.

5. Credit bureaus (if identity theft is a concern)
Canada has national credit bureaus (Equifax Canada and TransUnion Canada). Fraud reporting guidance often includes checking your credit report and asking about a fraud alert.

Also tell a trusted person and your adult learning staff if you want support while you report. You are not alone — scams are common, and calm reporting is the goal.

Bookmark: antifraudcentre.ca and the CRA scam pages on canada.ca.
